nodes.label: Network switch
nodes.description: Multiport network bridge that receives and forwards data toward destination devices using packet switching.

nodes.label: Ethernet switch
nodes.description: The most common form of network switch, typically providing Ethernet Layer 2 bridging.

nodes.label: Switching hub
nodes.description: Alternative name listed for a network switch.

nodes.label: Bridging hub
nodes.description: Alternative name listed for a network switch.

nodes.label: MAC bridge
nodes.description: IEEE terminology for a network switch operating on MAC addresses at Layer 2.

nodes.label: Multiport bridge
nodes.description: Bridge with multiple interfaces that forwards frames based on learned hardware addresses.

nodes.label: OSI Layer 1 — Physical
nodes.description: Physical signaling and interfaces needed to carry bits over a medium; the source says Layer 1 functionality is required in all switches.

nodes.label: OSI Layer 2 — Data Link
nodes.description: Layer at which Ethernet switching and MAC-address-based bridging operate.

nodes.label: OSI Layer 3 — Network
nodes.description: Layer where IP routing can be incorporated into Layer 3 or multilayer switches.

nodes.label: OSI Layer 4 — Transport
nodes.description: Transport-layer protocols above IP; not the ordinary forwarding basis of a Layer 2 switch.

nodes.label: OSI model
nodes.description: Layered conceptual model used to distinguish physical, data-link, network and higher-layer functions.

nodes.label: Packet switching
nodes.description: Receive and forward data in packets/frames rather than blindly repeating all signals to every port.

nodes.label: Ethernet frame
nodes.description: Layer 2 unit whose header carries information used for switching decisions.

nodes.label: Network packet
nodes.description: General term used in the article for received and forwarded network data; exact PDU terminology depends on layer.

nodes.label: MAC address
nodes.description: Hardware/link-layer address used by Layer 2 switches to learn devices and forward frames.

nodes.label: MAC address table
nodes.description: Mapping from learned MAC addresses to switch ports; often implemented with CAM.

nodes.label: Content-addressable memory (CAM)
nodes.description: High-speed memory often used to implement the MAC address/CAM table for address lookup.

nodes.label: Switch port
nodes.description: Physical or logical interface where a network device or link connects to a switch.

nodes.label: Collision domain
nodes.description: Segment in which Ethernet transmission collisions can occur under shared/half-duplex conditions.

nodes.label: Broadcast domain
nodes.description: Scope within which Layer 2 broadcast traffic is propagated; ordinary switches continue to forward broadcasts within the domain.

nodes.label: Local area network (LAN)
nodes.description: Network environment in which switches commonly connect hosts and other switches.

nodes.label: Wide area network (WAN)
nodes.description: Larger network scope; switches may be placed between WAN routers for monitoring or analysis.

nodes.label: Network host
nodes.description: End device connected to a network through a switch port.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.description: Device traditionally associated with Layer 3 interconnection and IP routing.

nodes.label: Layer 3 switch
nodes.description: Multilayer switch combining Layer 2 switching with network-layer routing functionality.

nodes.label: Multilayer switch
nodes.description: Switch that performs functions at Layer 2 and one or more higher OSI layers.

nodes.label: Repeater hub
nodes.description: Device that repeats received traffic out other ports without learning destination MAC addresses.

nodes.label: Point-to-point link
nodes.description: Dedicated connection between a device and switch port, allowing independent transmissions on separate ports.

nodes.label: Full-duplex mode
nodes.description: Mode where a port can transmit and receive simultaneously when both endpoints support it.

nodes.label: Half-duplex mode
nodes.description: Mode where a port can transmit or receive at a given time, not both simultaneously.

nodes.label: Micro-segmentation
nodes.description: Extreme segmentation in which each device has a dedicated switch port and collision domain.

nodes.label: Network segmentation
nodes.description: Use of switches to divide a larger collision domain into smaller domains to reduce collisions and improve throughput.

nodes.label: Network throughput
nodes.description: Amount of data transferred over time; affected by dedicated bandwidth, uplinks, buffering and congestion.

nodes.label: Network latency
nodes.description: Time for a frame to traverse switching; cut-through switching can reduce switch latency.

nodes.label: Link bandwidth
nodes.description: Transmission capacity of a port or link; input and output port rates may differ.

nodes.label: Packet/frame buffer
nodes.description: Storage used to hold incoming frames while adapting to output-port transmission speed.

nodes.label: Frame forwarding
nodes.description: Decision and action that send a frame toward the port associated with its destination MAC address.

nodes.label: Unknown-destination/broadcast flooding
nodes.description: Forwarding to multiple eligible ports when traffic is not directed to a single learned destination or is broadcast; details depend on frame type and VLAN.

nodes.label: MAC learning
nodes.description: Switch learns which MAC address is reachable through which port and records the mapping.

nodes.label: Unknown unicast
nodes.description: Unicast frame whose destination MAC is not currently known in the forwarding table; commonly flooded within its Layer 2 domain.

nodes.label: Virtual LAN (VLAN)
nodes.description: Logical Layer 2 segmentation configured on managed switches; VLAN assignments and 802.1Q tagging are management features.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.1Q
nodes.description: Standard associated with VLAN tagging.

nodes.label: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)
nodes.description: Loop-prevention protocol that disables forwarding on selected links so the active Layer 2 topology forms a tree.

nodes.label: Shortest Path Bridging (SPB)
nodes.description: Layer 2 alternative to STP described as permitting active paths and multiple equal-cost paths.

nodes.label: TRILL
nodes.description: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links; Layer 2 alternative to STP described as permitting all paths to be active with multiple equal-cost paths.

nodes.label: Layer 2 switching loop
nodes.description: Forwarding cycle that Layer 2 loop-prevention/topology mechanisms seek to prevent.

nodes.label: Link aggregation
nodes.description: Combines multiple ports into one logical connection for higher transfer rates and reliability.

nodes.label: Quality of Service (QoS)
nodes.description: Configuration and monitoring of traffic service priorities or treatment.

nodes.label: Access control list (ACL)
nodes.description: Rules that can constrain traffic or access; managed switches may offer ACL features.

nodes.label: MAC filtering
nodes.description: Access-control feature based on MAC addresses.

nodes.label: Power over Ethernet (PoE)
nodes.description: Switch supplies electrical power over Ethernet to connected devices such as VoIP phones and wireless access points.

nodes.label: Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)
nodes.description: Backup power source that can keep a switch and attached devices operating during ordinary office power loss.

nodes.label: Network interface controller (NIC)
nodes.description: Endpoint/network interface connecting a host to the link; it participates in link-layer frame transmission and reception.

nodes.label: Small Form-factor Pluggable (SFP)
nodes.description: Pluggable transceiver/module format used to connect a switch to physical media such as fiber.

nodes.label: Direct Attach Copper (DAC) cable
nodes.description: Copper cable that can be used instead of a pluggable optical module in supported configurations.

nodes.label: Network transceiver
nodes.description: Converts between device-side electrical/optical signals and a physical link medium.

nodes.label: Fiber-optic cable
nodes.description: Optical transmission medium connected through transceivers or related optics.

nodes.label: Copper cable
nodes.description: Electrical transmission medium, including DAC cables and copper Ethernet cabling.

nodes.label: Co-packaged optics (CPO)

nodes.label: Pluggable optical module

nodes.description: On a switched network, ordinary endpoints see traffic for their own sending/receiving ports rather than all traffic on other ports.

nodes.label: Power supplied to endpoint

source_claims.claim: A network switch is a multiport bridge that forwards traffic toward destination devices, typically using MAC addresses at Layer 2.
Unlike a repeater hub, a switch learns device addresses and forwards data toward the destination port rather than repeating everything to all ports.
Each switch port forms a separate collision domain in the described Ethernet model, while broadcasts remain within the broadcast domain.
Switches may use SFP and other pluggable transceiver modules, DAC cables and co-packaged optics.
Some switches add Layer 3 routing and are called Layer 3 or multilayer switches.
The MAC address table maps MAC addresses to ports and is often implemented with high-speed CAM.
Cut-through switches may begin forwarding before the entire frame payload has arrived, reducing latency.
STP disables forwarding on selected links to avoid switching loops; SPB and TRILL are described as alternatives supporting active paths.
PoE can power endpoints such as VoIP phones and wireless access points; UPS-backed switch power can support continuity.
Managed switch features include VLANs, link aggregation, QoS, ACLs, SNMP, port mirroring, NTP, 802.1X, LLDP and IGMP snooping.
Port mirroring sends a copy of selected traffic to a monitoring port; alternatives include SMON, RMON, sFlow, a network tap or a Layer 1 hub.
The article credits Mark Kempf/DEC with the 1983 MAC bridge and dates Kalpana's seven-port EtherSwitch to 1989–1990.
The article warns that its lead may be too technical for most readers.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Managed models expose configuration and monitoring; unmanaged models are plug-and-play.
Smart switches offer limited controls; enterprise switches expose broader CLI/SNMP/web management and configuration lifecycle features.
Port mirroring copies traffic within switch configuration; a tap is an external hardware monitoring method.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Explains visibility methods and failure domains.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Cut-through starts forwarding before the full payload arrives; buffering/store-forward waits longer but can support different handling.
STP forms a loop-free tree by disabling selected links; SPB/TRILL are described as alternatives allowing multiple paths active.
A VLAN is logical segmentation; a port is a physical/logical interface and may be assigned to a VLAN.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates logical topology from physical interface.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: An optical module/transceiver connects an interface to fiber; a supported DAC cable can replace a module for copper connectivity.
PoE delivers power over Ethernet to endpoints; UPS provides backup power to the switch/power system.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Traditional Layer 2 switching bridges MAC-addressed frames; routers interconnect at Layer 3; multilayer switches may combine functions.

misconceptions.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
misconceptions.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.
Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

misconceptions.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

misconceptions.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

misconceptions.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
misconceptions.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

misconceptions.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
misconceptions.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

misconceptions.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
misconceptions.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

misconceptions.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
misconceptions.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

misconceptions.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

misconceptions.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
misconceptions.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

misconceptions.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
misconceptions.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

misconceptions.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
misconceptions.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

misconceptions.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
misconceptions.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

misconceptions.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
misconceptions.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.
